questions.q: On Map 1 in the NCERT textbook, which of the following sites is NOT located in the Sarasvati (Ghaggar-Hakra) basin: Rakhigarhi, Banawali, Kalibangan, or Mohenjodaro?
questions.a: Correct answer: Mohenjodaro. It lies on the right bank of the Indus River in Sindh, Pakistan, well west of the Sarasvati basin. Rakhigarhi (Hisar, Haryana), Banawali (Fatehabad, Haryana), and Kalibangan (Hanumangarh, Rajasthan) are all situated along the Ghaggar-Hakra palaeochannel. A student who selects Kalibangan may be confusing the Ghaggar-Hakra with the Indus tributaries; Kalibangan is on the left bank of the Ghaggar, not the Indus.

questions.q: The NCERT states that "nearly two-thirds of these settlements are in the Sarasvati basin." If a student claims this proves the Sarasvati was the *only* river that mattered to the Harappans, what key geographical evidence from Map 1 contradicts this overstatement?
questions.a: The presence of major urban centres like Mohenjodaro (Indus), Dholavira (Luni/Rann of Kutch), Lothal (Sabarmati/Gulf of Khambhat), Sutkagendor (Makran coast), and Shortughai (Oxus/Amu Darya in Afghanistan) demonstrates that Harappan settlement was multi-riverine and coastal, not mono-basin. The Sarasvati basin had the highest *density* of sites, but the civilisation's economic reach extended to the Indus delta, Gujarat coast, and Central Asian lapis lazuli sources. A student making this claim is conflating "highest density" with "exclusive importance."

questions.q: Using Map 1, explain why Dholavira (Gujarat) and Lothal (Gujarat) are classified as "ports" or "coastal centres" despite being far from the open Arabian Sea today. What geographical change must be inferred?
questions.a: During the Mature Harappan period, sea level was higher (mid-Holocene highstand) and the Rann of Kutch was a navigable gulf, not a seasonal salt marsh. Dholavira sits on Khadir Bet island in the Great Rann, and Lothal lies at the head of the Gulf of Khambhat; both had direct tidal access to the Arabian Sea. A student who answers "they were on rivers" misses the marine archaeology evidence (dockyard at Lothal, massive reservoirs at Dholavira for rainwater harvesting in a saline environment) and the palaeogeographic reconstruction of the coastline.

questions.q: Compare the site distribution in the Sarasvati basin (Map 1) with the Early Harappan cultures shown on Map 2 (Amri-Nal, Kot Diji, Damb Sadaat, Siswal). What does the spatial overlap suggest about the transition from Early to Mature Harappan?
questions.a: The Mature Harappan sites densely occupy the same geographical corridor (Ghaggar-Hakra plains) where Early Harappan cultures (Siswal, Kot Diji) were already established. This indicates *in situ* urbanisation — the Mature phase emerged from local Early Harappan roots through gradual internal development, not sudden migration or external conquest. A student who sees a "break" or "invasion" is ignoring the continuity in settlement location, subsistence base (wheat/barley), and material culture (pottery traditions) documented in the NCERT.

questions.q: A competitive exam question asks: "Which Harappan site provides the strongest evidence for the civilisation's connection to the lapis lazuli trade with Afghanistan?" Evaluate the options: (a) Harappa, (b) Mohenjodaro, (c) Shortughai, (d) Lothal. Justify your choice using geographical reasoning.
questions.a: Correct answer: (c) Shortughai. It is located in northern Afghanistan near the Badakhshan lapis lazuli mines — the *only* known source in the ancient world. Its position on the Oxus River allowed direct procurement and downstream transport to the Indus plains. Harappa and Mohenjodaro are consumer sites 1,500 km away; Lothal is a maritime gateway for Gulf/Mesopotamia trade. A student choosing Harappa because "it's a big city" fails to distinguish between *production/procurement* sites and *consumption/redistribution* centres.

questions.q: Construct a 3-tier hierarchy of Mature Harappan settlements based on Map 1 and the NCERT description, giving one example per tier and the functional criterion for each tier.
questions.a: Tier 1 – Major Urban Centres (>100 ha): Rakhigarhi (550 ha) — administrative/ritual/craft hub with citadel, granary, Great Bath. Tier 2 – Regional Centres / Specialised Production Sites (10–50 ha): Chanhudaro (7 ha, craft production), Kalibangan (fire altars, ploughed field), Nageshwar/Balakot (shell working). Tier 3 – Agricultural Villages / Ports / Outposts (<10 ha): Lothal (port, bead factory), Sutkagendor (coastal trade), Shortughai (lapis lazuli procurement), Rangpur (rice cultivation). Criterion: size + functional specialisation + architectural complexity. A flat list without functional differentiation shows incomplete analysis.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: The Mature Harappan phase (2600–1900 BCE) represents the urban zenith of the Harappan Civilisation, ______ by a vast, integrated cultural zone spanning approximately 1.5 million sq. km across the Indus and Sarasvati (Ghaggar-Hakra) river systems.

Fill in the blank: Imagine you are standing at the ______ mound in Hisar, Haryana — the largest Harappan city at 550 hectares — and you look north toward the dry bed of the Ghaggar river (identified as the Vedic Sarasvati).

Fill in the blank: Imagine you are standing at the Rakhigarhi mound in Hisar, Haryana — the largest Harappan city at ______ hectares — and you look north toward the dry bed of the Ghaggar river (identified as the Vedic Sarasvati).
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can (1) locate and label all five major Mature Harappan cities and at least ten secondary sites on an outline map of the subcontinent, (2) explain the strategic relationship between site distribution and the Indus-Sarasvati riverine network, and (3) evaluate why the Sarasvati basin hosted a higher density of settlements than.
